report.source_text: On examination, she had widespread thickening of the skin predominantly involving the trunk and proximal extremities (Fig. 1). She did not have sclerodactyly, but she had deformities in keeping with osteoarthritis (Fig. 2). She denied cold-induced episodic acral bluish discoloration suggestive of Raynaud’s phenomenon. She was not febrile, and the result of her general examination was normal without pallor, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or bilateral ankle edema. Her respiratory and cardiovascular examination results were normal with a heart rate of 82 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 130/80 mmHg. The result of her neurological examination was normal with normal funduscopy without any cranial neuropathy or peripheral neuropathy. Repeated echocardiography did not reveal any evidence of pulmonary hypertension. Upper gastroduodenoscopy did not show reflux disease. Radiographically, there was no evidence of interstitial lung disease.

clinician.final_diagnosis: scleredema type 2 associated with IgA-κ smoldering myeloma
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 66-year-old woman with a 34-year history of diffuse skin thickening initially diagnosed as systemic sclerosis but lacking typical antibody profile or Raynaud’s phenomenon had skin biopsies revealing histopathologic features of scleredema. Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrated a monoclonal band with paraprotein level at 8.9 g/dl. Bone marrow biopsy showed 15% monoclonal plasma cells without end organ damage, consistent with smoldering myeloma. This evidence revised the diagnosis to scleredema type 2 associated with IgA-κ smoldering myeloma.
